patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Nunavut → France: Fr Johannes Rivoire; Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011); Vancouver → Long Island, New York: Fr Damian Cooper; Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince; Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore; Newfoundland → British Columbia: Brother Edward English.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Mount Cashel Orphanage: first report 1975, first action 1989 (14 years). Royal Newfoundland Constabulary probe opened Dec 1975 was closed by the police chief nine days later; the Justice Department ordered the report rewritten (1976); Deputy Minister of Justice said further action unwarranted (1977) Graham James (hockey): first report 1996, first action 1997 (1 years). Received a federal pardon in 2007 that became public only in 2010
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.0 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Ontario 2016: Bill 132 (Royal Assent 9 March 2016) removed limitation periods for civil claims based on sexual assault/abuse
patterns.pattern_summary: Most survivors disclose decades later, after the legal deadline to sue or prosecute has passed. Where legislatures tried to lift those deadlines, the institutions facing claims lobbied against it, and when the deadlines fell, many filed for bankruptcy. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018; in Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million and the insurance federation nearly $20.7 million from 2014 to 2024. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and orders filed for bankruptcy, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1989: Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Response of the Newfoundland Criminal Justice System (Hughes Inquiry), 1989-1992. Officials had transferred offenders and covered up abuse; 11 Christian Brothers convicted; Newfoundland paid C$11.5m compensation in 1996
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Msgr Carlo Alberto Capella, Holy See nunciature in Washington: Convicted by a Vatican tribunal 2018: five years and a €5,000 fine — not tried in the US or Canada
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Canada on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans (receiving or involved). Canada — Sixties Scoop: Ontario ruling 2017 and C$800m settlement. Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims. Canada — maternity homes and post-war adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 1997: Canada: Criminal Code extraterritorial child sex tourism provisions (Bill C-27 in force 26 May 1997; Bill C-15A 23 July 2002); up to 14 years
patterns.pattern_summary: Child sex tourism followed enforcement around the map. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. When Manila closed Ermita in 1992, businesses moved to Angeles City. Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). Then the trade moved online: in the Philippines, street and establishment child sex trafficking fell 79–86% in targeted cities (2006–2016), while monthly Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold (2014–2017).

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Childs Play — run by Australia's Task Force Argos for 11 months (police ran abuse sites to catch users). Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined (claimed, not established).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: the founder of Colonia Dignidad in Chile was convicted of abusing children there and charged with aiding the Pinochet regime, which Chilean officials say used the colony to torture opponents, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Banks and firms fined, sued or settled
patterns.role_note: Aylo (Pornhub owner) — DOJ deferred prosecution: Deferred prosecution agreement (21 Dec 2023, Brooklyn) over unlawful monetary transactions involving sex-trafficking proceeds (GirlsDoPorn — adult victims); paid over $1.8m plus victim compensation
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Graham James — junior hockey coach (Western Hockey League)
cases.who: Graham James (coach/GM, Swift Current Broncos, Calgary Hitmen)
cases.what: James was convicted in 1997 of sexually assaulting three junior players he coached, and sentenced to 3½ years. After a former player's 2009 memoir and police complaint, he pleaded guilty in Dec 2011 to molesting two more players when they were teenagers; the two-year sentence was raised to five years by the Manitoba Court of Appeal in Feb 2013.
cases.cover_up: He received a federal pardon in 2007, which became public in 2010.

cases.title: Rev. Gordon Nakayama — Anglican dioceses of New Westminster and Calgary
cases.who: Anglican Church of Canada; Japanese Canadian congregations
cases.what: Gordon Goichi Nakayama served for more than 50 years as an Anglican priest to Japanese Canadian communities in the dioceses of Calgary and New Westminster. In 1994 he admitted a history of sexually abusing minors and shortly before his death in 1995 signed a written confession to Archbishop Barry Curtis; he was charged with immorality under church law and resigned from ministry, but police were not told. On 15 June 2015 the two dioceses formally apologised to survivors in Vancouver. The church said it is not known how many minors were abused.
cases.cover_up: Nakayama made a written confession in 1994; the dioceses did not report it to police. He was allowed to resign and died in 1995.

cases.title: Canada — Ideal Maternity Home ('Butterbox Babies'), Nova Scotia
cases.who: William Peach Young and Lila Gladys Young
cases.what: The Ideal Maternity Home in Nova Scotia, run by William and Lila Young from the late 1920s until 1947, promised discreet birthing and adoption for unmarried mothers. According to author Bette Cahill, people paid up to $10,000, usually disguised as a donation, to adopt babies from the home, while babies considered 'unmarketable' were fed only molasses and water; many died and were buried in butter boxes. Wikipedia, citing Cahill, adds that mothers were charged $500, that the provincial Department of Public Welfare gathered evidence from 1934, and that the Youngs were convicted of fraud in 1935, acquitted of manslaughter in 1936, and convicted in 1946 on seven violations of the Maternity Boarding Houses Act; a 1946 Montreal Standard article described their 'baby farm rackets'.

cases.title: Fr Johannes Rivoire — Oblate in Nunavut, never extradited from France
cases.who: Oblates of Mary Immaculate (OMI Lacombe Canada; Oblates of France)
cases.what: French Oblate Johannes Rivoire worked in the Canadian North from 1959 to 1993. He faced at least three sexual-abuse charges (1998 warrant) concerning Inuit children in Arviat, Rankin Inlet and Naujaat, and a 2022 warrant for indecent assault on a girl in Arviat and Whale Cove between 1974 and 1979. A March 2024 review by retired Quebec justice André Denis, commissioned by the Oblates, concluded on the preponderance of evidence that he assaulted six children. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami called his death without trial in April 2024 'a systemic failure of nation states and religious institutions'.
cases.cover_up: He left for France in January 1993; a Canadian arrest warrant followed in 1998 and charges were later stayed. A 2022 warrant led to an extradition request that French authorities denied. The 2024 Denis review found the RCMP never contacted the Oblates when charges were laid. In February 2024 the Vatican ruled against his dismissal. He died in France in 2024 without trial.

cases.title: Mount Cashel Orphanage, St John's — Hughes Royal Commission
cases.who: Mount Cashel Orphanage run by the Irish Christian Brothers, with privileged foster-home status from Newfoundland Social Services; Royal Newfoundland Constabulary; provincial Department of Justice
cases.what: Complaints of abuse at Mount Cashel surfaced in 1974 and 1975 but neither led to charges. Police reopened the case in February 1989; nine Christian Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission (156 hearing days, over 200 witnesses, report 31 May 1991) found neither the police nor the Justice Department handled the 1975–76 files normally, and that child welfare director Frank Simms insisted on special treatment for the Brothers. The province paid $11 million to more than 40 victims in 1997.
cases.cover_up: In December 1975 the police chief and assistant chief ordered Detective Robert Hillier to end his investigation after two Brothers admitted molestation; references to sexual assault were removed and the first report destroyed. The Justice Department laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Canada — Sixties Scoop: Ontario ruling 2017 and C$800m settlement
cases.who: Federal government of Canada and provincial child welfare authorities
cases.what: From the 1950s into the 1980s thousands of Indigenous children were taken from their families by child welfare authorities and placed with non-Indigenous foster and adoptive families. On 14 February 2017 Justice Edward Belobaba of the Ontario Superior Court (Brown v. Canada) ruled that Ottawa had failed in its duty of care to on-reserve children in Ontario removed between 1965 and 1984, who lost their language, culture and identity; the class was expected to number about 16,000. On 6 October 2017 Crown-Indigenous Affairs Minister Carolyn Bennett announced an agreement in principle worth about C$800 million: C$750 million for First Nations and Inuit people removed between 1951 and 1991 (C$25,000 each if there were more than 20,000 claimants, up to C$50,000 if fewer) and C$50 million for a reconciliation and healing foundation.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans
cases.who: US government (Military Airlift Command); Holt International, Friends of Children of Viet Nam, Friends For All Children and other agencies
cases.what: In April 1975, as South Vietnam was falling, President Ford directed that a $2 million special foreign aid fund be used to fly 2,000 South Vietnamese orphans to the United States; Wikipedia, citing several sources, gives a total of over 3,300 children airlifted. The first flight, a C-5 cargo plane, crash-landed shortly after take-off on 4 April 1975, killing many of the children on board (78, according to US Defense Intelligence Agency figures cited by Wikipedia). A lawsuit filed against Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, the federal government and the adoption agencies argued that many of the children were not orphans and had been given up under duress during wartime; poor families sometimes placed children in orphanages without intending to give them up, and many adoption records lacked parental consent.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Canada — maternity homes and post-war adoptions of unmarried mothers' babies
cases.who: Maternity homes run mostly by the Catholic Church and the Salvation Army, some Anglican and United Church; Children's Aid Societies
cases.what: Women sent to maternity homes for unwed mothers after the Second World War say they were coerced into giving up babies they wanted to keep through shaming, intimidation and withholding information about alternatives such as social assistance; one woman later found her file recorded that she had wanted to take her baby home. Origins Canada asked the churches to support a parliamentary or Senate inquiry (Anglican Journal, May 2014).

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims
cases.who: Government of Canada; schools operated by the Catholic, Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
cases.what: About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended federally funded, church-run residential schools; the last closed in 1997. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's final report (December 2015) documented 3,200 deaths and said the true number is much higher. By the end of 2014, 37,951 claims had been made for injuries from physical and sexual abuse and 30,939 resolved. The Independent Assessment Process received 38,276 claims in total; adjudicators awarded $2.14 billion to 23,431 claimants and the government compensated 4,415 more directly.
cases.cover_up: Under the settlement, claimants' IAP records are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep or share them.

flows.title: Seoul → Canada
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Canada; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: UK → Canada child migrants (Home Children)
flows.what: British child migration to Canada began in the 19th century; IICSA found the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to sexual abuse allegations at its schools in Canada.

flows.title: Czech-produced abuse images → buyers in the EU and Canada
flows.what: A Czech photographer and Swedish partner distributed images of about 70 children to customers abroad.

flows.title: Films made in Ukraine/Romania → distributed by Azov Films, Toronto
flows.what: Primary producers were in Crimea (Ukraine), Romania and Germany; the Toronto firm sold to customers in over 50 countries. Start year approximate.

flows.title: Canada → Nepal (aid-worker offender)
flows.what: A Canadian humanitarian working with street children abused boys at his home in Nepal.

flows.title: Nunavut → France: Fr Johannes Rivoire
flows.what: Rivoire left the Arctic for France in January 1993; Canadian warrants (1998, 2022) went unexecuted and France refused extradition. He died in France in 2024.

flows.title: Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011)
flows.what: About to be charged in 1995, the Oblate fled to Belgium; Oblate officials acknowledged knowing he was leaving, and he lived 16 years in Oblate houses despite an international warrant until returned in 2011. In 2015 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children in Igloolik (1978–82).

flows.title: Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore
flows.what: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore, later convicted (2018) of abusing three children and a student priest, to Toronto and to Fort Augustus.

IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
cases.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
cases.what: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.

cases.title: France — state report finds 'illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption
cases.who: French government and adoption associations
cases.what: In March 2024 France released an assessment acknowledging that its government had long known of 'the existence of illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption, and that diplomatic and association archives showed these practices existed in countries over long periods. France received 11,165 Korean children 1968–2008 among others.
cases.cover_up: The report said public authorities were alerted early, including at the highest levels, and were late in taking action.

cases.title: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
cases.who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
cases.what: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Nth Room and Doctor's Room — Telegram sexual blackmail rings
cases.who: Telegram chatrooms 'Nth Room' (Moon Hyung-wook) and 'Doctor's Room' (Cho Ju-bin)
cases.what: Operators blackmailed women and girls into producing sexual images and videos and sold access to Telegram chatrooms; at least 10,000 people used the 'Doctor's Room' chats, some paying up to $1,200. At least 74 victims, including 16 minors, were exploited there. After petitions signed by millions, police named the operator, Cho Ju-bin, in March 2020 — the first official identity disclosure for a sex offender in South Korea — and on 26 November 2020 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to 40 years (reported raised to 42 years on appeal in 2021). Moon Hyung-wook, who created the original 'Nth Room' chatrooms, was sentenced to 34 years by the Andong court on 8 April 2021. The law was changed to punish possessing and viewing such material.
cases.cover_up: A man's early 112 report was reportedly not treated as credible (Wikipedia, citation needed); two university students ('Team Flame') and journalists exposed it in 2019.

cases.title: South Korea school deepfake crisis on Telegram (2024)
cases.who: Telegram group chats creating sexual deepfakes of classmates and teachers
cases.what: In August 2024 a journalist's reporting revealed Telegram chatrooms, some dedicated to specific high schools and middle schools, where users made and shared sexual deepfakes of female students, teachers and others; one room for pupils at a single school had more than 2,000 members. Within a week activists had identified more than 500 schools and universities as targets. Police said they had handled more than 800 deepfake sex crime cases in 2024 by late September, against 156 in all of 2021, and that most victims and perpetrators were teenagers. On 26 September 2024 the National Assembly passed a bill criminalising possessing or watching sexual deepfakes; earlier that month police opened an investigation into whether Telegram was complicit.

cases.title: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
cases.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
cases.what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

cases.title: Gwangju Inhwa School for the deaf — the 'Dogani' case
cases.who: Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students (founded 1961; principal was the founder's son)
cases.what: A 2005 investigation found that six people at the school, including the headmaster, had sexually harassed or raped at least nine deaf students from 2000 onward. Four received prison terms, two of which were later suspended; two escaped punishment because the statute of limitations had expired. After the 2011 film 'Silenced' (Dogani), police opened a new investigation, the city moved to close the school in November 2011, and on 28 Oct 2011 the National Assembly passed the 'Dogani Law' removing the statute of limitations for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people. In July 2012 a former administrator was sentenced to 12 years for sexually assaulting an 18-year-old student in April 2005.
cases.cover_up: The teacher who alerted human rights groups in 2005 was fired; police acted only four months later after former students went to national TV; the city government and school board passed the case back and forth; appeal courts cut sentences to probation and four of the six teachers were reinstated.

cases.title: South Korea — runaway children in commercial sex; police officer convicted (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Entertainment establishments, escort services, chat-room operators
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit South Korean women and children, including runaways, in bars, nightclubs and internet-advertised escort services, and chat-room operators coerce children with compromising images into producing sexual material. A court convicted a local police officer in a 2022 case involving alleged complicity in trafficking-related crimes and sentenced him to five years; another officer was acquitted.
cases.cover_up: NGOs previously reported some local police sexually exploited children; one officer was convicted (bribery, secrecy violations) and another acquitted.

cases.title: Mongolia — girls sex-trafficked in Ulaanbaatar hotels and karaoke bars (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers in hotels, massage parlours, karaoke clubs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and border areas, sometimes facilitated by a lack of police enforcement; traffickers use online platforms to groom and blackmail children; and children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, e.g. as horse jockeys.
cases.cover_up: The report says exploitation is sometimes facilitated by lack of police enforcement; some families are complicit.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2025: report: Swedish state inquiry report on intercountry adoption (2 June 2025)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 6,820 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (2% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, Puebla police arrested the journalist who exposed a Cancún abuse ring, and leaked calls recorded the state governor discussing her jailing; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law
cases.who: Greek state institutions and foundling homes; AHEPA and other US agencies and proxy-adoption intermediaries
cases.what: Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many called 'orphans' after the civil war or born 'illegitimate', were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures. A law published on 2 May 2025 recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to records. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s that has not been carried out.
cases.cover_up: The adoptions were covered by confidentiality and secrecy; many adoptees lacked papers proving their origins.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Sweden; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.what: Sri Lankan children adopted to Sweden in the 1980s (baby-farm period).

flows.what: Children taken from Chilean mothers and adopted in Sweden, peaking under Pinochet; Sweden opened its own inquiry.

flows.title: Athens → Sweden
flows.what: Greek-born children adopted to Sweden 1950–1975; Greece restored their citizenship by law on 2 May 2025.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Tehuacán → Los Angeles → Mexico: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera; Costa Rica → Mexico: Fr Mauricio Víquez (flight, extradited 2021).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Jean Succar Kuri (Cancún): first report 2003, first action 2004 (1 years). Journalist Lydia Cacho, who exposed the ring and links to businessman Kamel Nacif, was arrested and harassed in 2005; Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6-4 in 2007 that Puebla governor Mario Marín had no case to answer; Marín was arrested for her alleged torture only in 2021 Marcial Maciel (Legion of Christ): first report 1976, first action 2006 (30 years). Juan Vaca's 1976 letter reached the Vatican; formal charges filed 1998 were not pursued by the CDF
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.0 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2020: Mexican Episcopal Conference self-report, Jan 2020. 426 priests investigated over ten years, 217 removed; El Universal: only 6 of 156 alleged child abuse cases 2009-2019 ended in conviction
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters; La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora; Jean Succar Kuri — Cancún child sexual exploitation ring; Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, Puebla police arrested the journalist who exposed a Cancún abuse ring, and leaked calls recorded the state governor discussing her jailing; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Costa Rica — Fr Mauricio Víquez, convicted after fleeing to Mexico
cases.who: Archdiocese of San José; Episcopal Conference of Costa Rica
cases.what: Víquez, a former church spokesman on family issues, fled Costa Rica in 2018 when accusations surfaced, going via Panama to San Nicolás de los Garza, Mexico, where he was caught; he was extradited in 2021. The church expelled him from the clergy in 2019. In March 2022 he was sentenced to 20 years (6 for sexual abuse, 14 for rape) for abusing an 11-year-old boy in his parish in 2002–2003. In August 2022 a civil court ordered the archbishop and two church entities to pay about US$100,000 in damages.
cases.cover_up: A San José civil court ordered Archbishop José Rafael Quirós, the Episcopal Conference and the church's property entity to pay 65 million colones; the victims' lawyer said the church knew from 2002 and did nothing. Three other complaints were declared time-barred.

cases.title: Mexican bishops' conference — 426 priests investigated
cases.who: Conferencia del Episcopado Mexicano
cases.what: On 14 January 2020 the Mexican Episcopal Conference said it was investigating 426 priests over the previous ten years: 271 cases of abuse of minors in church settings and 155 other proceedings. It said 217 priests had been removed from their duties. El Universal reported in February 2020 that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into such sexual offences by religious figures from 2009 to 2019, but four prosecutors' offices recorded only six sentences.
cases.cover_up: El Universal reported only six convictions out of 156 alleged abuse cases involving minors, 2009–2019

cases.title: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters
cases.who: Iglesia Cristiana Restaurada (Restored Christian Church) shelters; Mexico City Attorney General's Office (PGJDF), which placed children there
cases.what: Children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the private Casitas del Sur shelter, run by a church group, went missing. In October 2010 Mexico's federal Attorney General offered rewards for information on 14 children who disappeared in February 2009 from the Casitas del Sur shelter in Mexico City and from related homes in Nuevo Laredo and Quintana Roo, and about 5 million pesos for three people sought in the case, saying the children may have been taken by child traffickers. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite the removal of 126 children by police and human rights staff on 29 January 2009 and obstruction charges against seven staff (not re-checked for this map).
cases.cover_up: A Mexico City legislator accused officials of the District Attorney's office of negligence and complicity, saying they warned the shelter of searches so children could be moved.

cases.title: La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora
cases.who: La Gran Familia shelter, founded 1947 by Rosa del Carmen Verduzco ('Mamá Rosa')
cases.what: On 15 July 2014 the PGR's organised-crime unit (SEIDO) raided the shelter and freed 432 children and 138 adults living in squalid conditions; the PGR said some had suffered sexual abuse, and residents reported rape, being held for years, food deprivation and forced begging. The PGR ruled out charging the 79-year-old founder because of age and mental decline; six others faced charges from unlawful imprisonment to organised crime. The PGR also investigated claims that the shelter in effect bought children through notarised parental waivers. Verduzco died in 2018.
cases.cover_up: More than 40 complaints from parents had been filed with Michoacán's DIF and the federal Attorney General's Office (PGR) before the raid.

cases.title: Jean Succar Kuri — Cancún child sexual exploitation ring
cases.who: Jean Succar Kuri (hotelier); associates named in Lydia Cacho's reporting
cases.what: Cancún hotel businessman Succar Kuri was detained in the United States (reported as Los Angeles/Arizona) in 2004 at the request of Mexico's federal prosecutors and Interpol, after complaints by several girls, and was later returned to Mexico. In 2011 a federal district court convicted him and sentenced him to 13 years; on appeal by both sides a Cancún appeals court raised the sentence to 112 years, which was upheld. In 2023 a federal circuit court annulled the 112-year sentence over procedural flaws and ordered a new ruling on sexual abuse and child pornography offences against seven minors, which reduced his term. He died in Cancún on 14 June 2024 while still serving his sentence. Journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' described him as the head of a child-exploitation network and linked him to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Governor Mario Marín.
cases.cover_up: See the related record on journalist Lydia Cacho's 2005 arrest arranged after her book exposed the ring.

cases.title: Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring
cases.who: Mario Marín (Governor of Puebla); Kamel Nacif Borge (businessman)
cases.what: After journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' (2005) linked Cancún businessman Jean Succar Kuri's child-exploitation network to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Puebla governor Mario Marín, Cacho was arrested in 2005 and says she was tortured. Arrest warrants for torture were issued against Marín and Nacif; Marín was arrested in Acapulco in February 2021, and Nacif was detained in Lebanon in May 2021 and later released there. Marín was moved to house arrest in August 2024, returned to prison in April 2025, and in July 2026 was again granted house arrest on health and age grounds while his trial for alleged torture of Cacho continues. Neither has been convicted; both are accused of torture, not of the abuse itself.
cases.cover_up: Intimidation of a journalist: after Cacho exposed the Cancún ring, Puebla police arrested her in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla. Leaked calls (La Jornada, 14 Feb 2006) recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her as a favour and having her abused in jail. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6–4 on 29 Nov 2007 that Marín had no case to answer.

cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. cases.cover_up: At hearings she threatened to reveal the names of politicians and powerful men she said were clients (her claim, unverified).

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Igloolik (Nunavut) → Belgium: Fr Eric Dejaeger (fugitive 1995–2011).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Marc Dutroux: first report 1995, first action 1996 (1 years). His mother wrote to authorities in 1995 that he was holding two girls; police took 14 months to arrest him although he was a prime suspect from June 1995; earlier released on parole after three years of a 1989 sentence
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.0 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2000: Commission for the handling of complaints of sexual abuse in a pastoral relationship (Halsberghe), 2000; second commission (Adriaenssens) 2009-2010. Halsberghe: 33 formal complaints, 32 upheld, most time-barred; Adriaenssens report Sept 2010: 475 complaints in six months, 13 suicides linked to clerical abuse, abusers in about 29 religious orders
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Belgium on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role: Welfare state, church and unmarried mothers
patterns.role_note: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role_note: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network (claimed, not established).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: the founder of Colonia Dignidad in Chile was convicted of abusing children there and charged with aiding the Pinochet regime, which Chilean officials say used the colony to torture opponents, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology; Dutroux affair — kidnap, abuse and murder of girls; police and justice failures.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network.
patterns.pattern_summary: Invented trafficking stories take resources from real ones. In July 2020 the US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about a false claim that the furniture seller Wayfair was selling children; the hotline's operator, Polaris, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed it, and none of the reports had new information. "Pizzagate" led to a man firing a rifle inside a Washington restaurant in 2016. London's Metropolitan Police spent over £2 million on Operation Midland, built on a "VIP ring" story invented by Carl Beech, who was himself jailed for child-abuse offences. The McMartin preschool trials in the 1980s cost about $15 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Dutroux 'X-dossiers' — witness claims of an elite abuse network
cases.who: Witnesses X1–X4 (claims); Belgian prosecutors
cases.what: Witnesses told investigators in 1996–97 of abuse parties and unsolved murders involving Marc Dutroux, Michel Nihoul and prominent people. Prosecutors ultimately dismissed the statements, and investigators were criticised for leading a key witness; an officer charged in 1997 with falsifying her statements was cleared in 1999. In 1999 the Guardian reported renewed cover-up claims, and that the parliamentary inquiry's chair said his findings had been muzzled. The claims of an elite network remain unproven; a 1999 book by three journalists argued the witnesses were more credible than portrayed.

cases.title: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology
cases.who: Flemish youth institutions, youth centres and boarding schools
cases.what: After clergy abuse cases, further cases emerged of child abuse in Flemish institutions between 1930 and 1990. A working group of experts led by child psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens, set up by Welfare Minister Jo Vandeurzen, produced two reports recognising the wide scope of abuse. On 23 April 2014 Flemish Parliament Speaker Jan Peumans formally apologised to victims of abuse in boarding schools and youth centres. A temporary recognition and mediation commission set up in 2014 was later made permanent; it received 121 reports in 2024.

cases.title: Dutroux affair — kidnap, abuse and murder of girls; police and justice failures
cases.who: Marc Dutroux, Michelle Martin, Michel Lelièvre; Belgian Gendarmerie and judicial police
cases.what: Dutroux, on parole for earlier rapes, kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19 in 1995–96; he was found guilty of kidnapping and raping all six, killing two and causing the deaths of two others. He was arrested in August 1996, and in October 1996 hundreds of thousands of Belgians joined the White March in Brussels to protest police and judicial failures. A parliamentary inquiry chaired by Marc Verwilghen sharply criticised the police investigation. On 22 June 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life; his ex-wife Michelle Martin got 30 years and Michel Lelièvre 25; businessman Michel Nihoul was acquitted of kidnapping and conspiracy but convicted of drug trafficking and other crimes (five years). Belgium later reorganised its police forces.
cases.cover_up: Dutroux was released early in 1992 from a 13.5-year sentence over prosecutor and psychiatrist objections. Police missed chances, including voices heard in his cellar and unreviewed videotapes; rivalry between Gendarmerie and judicial police hampered the hunt. Judge Connerotte was removed in Oct 1996 for attending a victims' fundraising dinner.

Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations

Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.what: In September 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and village clinic doctors and nurses, for 'abuse of power and authority'. They allegedly solicited infants from poor families and falsified documents saying the babies were abandoned; 266 babies were sent for foreign adoption from 2005 to July 2008. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi had reported desertion numbers rising 17-fold or more at orphanages in 7 provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the US when it expired in September 2008.

cases.title: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans
cases.who: US government (Military Airlift Command); Holt International, Friends of Children of Viet Nam, Friends For All Children and other agencies
cases.what: In April 1975, as South Vietnam was falling, President Ford directed that a $2 million special foreign aid fund be used to fly 2,000 South Vietnamese orphans to the United States; Wikipedia, citing several sources, gives a total of over 3,300 children airlifted. The first flight, a C-5 cargo plane, crash-landed shortly after take-off on 4 April 1975, killing many of the children on board (78, according to US Defense Intelligence Agency figures cited by Wikipedia). A lawsuit filed against Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, the federal government and the adoption agencies argued that many of the children were not orphans and had been given up under duress during wartime; poor families sometimes placed children in orphanages without intending to give them up, and many adoption records lacked parental consent.

cases.title: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
cases.who: Baby 101 company
cases.what: In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held in two Bangkok houses with passports confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking; four said they had been tricked, and the health minister said some appeared to have been raped.

flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Hanoi, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 828 in FY2007).

flows.title: Gary Glitter: UK → Cambodia → Vietnam
flows.what: After his 1999 UK conviction, Paul Gadd moved to Cambodia (expelled 2002–03) and then Vietnam, where he was convicted in 2006 of obscene acts with girls aged 10 and 11.
