patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa').
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Zimbabwe — sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines; girls traded under ngozi (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, Puebla police arrested the journalist who exposed a Cancún abuse ring, and leaked calls recorded the state governor discussing her jailing; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cases.what: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
cases.cover_up: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Zimbabwe — sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines; girls traded under ngozi (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers at mining sites; families
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and children in sex trafficking around mines, sometimes for money or food, and may exploit children as panners and ore couriers in gold and diamond mines. Traditional practices including trading daughters for food or money and ngozi — giving a relative to another family to atone for a killing — make girls vulnerable. Low-level official complicity persisted.

flows.title: UK → Southern Rhodesia child migrants (Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College)
flows.what: IICSA found that children who told the headmaster they had been sexually abused by a padre at the college were beaten and warned against 'spreading malicious lies'; it lacked evidence to say whether Fairbridge UK knew of the allegations.

flows.title: England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa')
flows.what: After the 1982 Ruston Report on his beatings was kept from police, Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 and founded Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986. The Makin Review called him 'a problem solved and exported to Africa'.

flows.title: Zimbabwe → South Africa (John Smyth)
flows.what: Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, Smyth moved to South Africa in 2001, attending churches in Durban (from 2002) and Cape Town (Church on Main, 2004–2016). The Makin Review found it highly likely he kept abusing until his death in 2018.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role_note: Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war, taking children is often a tactic. The UN commission on Syria found in 2016 that ISIS sold Yazidi girls in markets as sexual slaves and that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls at Chibok in 2014; 82 were still captive a decade later. The International Criminal Court convicted the LRA commander Dominic Ongwen on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, with girls as young as eight. The UN's yearly children-and-armed-conflict reports verify these attacks country by country.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017 (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: the founder of Colonia Dignidad in Chile was convicted of abusing children there and charged with aiding the Pinochet regime, which Chilean officials say used the colony to torture opponents, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: The map's documented record is thickest where people looked. Childlight's 2026 update rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries; South Asia, West and Central Africa and the Middle East and North Africa lack them. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.

cases.title: Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified)
cases.who: Taliban de facto authorities
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 12 children (6 boys, 6 girls) in Afghanistan in 2023, 10 attributed to the Taliban, and the abduction of 3 children by the Taliban for sexual violence purposes. It verified 13 cases in 2022 (Taliban 7) and 6 in 2024 (Taliban 5).

cases.title: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017
cases.who: Afghan National Defense and Security Forces and Afghan Local Police commanders; US military chain of command
cases.what: In September 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told to ignore sexual abuse of boys by Afghan allies, describing it as rampant; nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) to investigate. SIGAR's report, sent to Congress in 2017 and made public on 23 January 2018, found that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault, and said 'the full extent of child sexual assault committed by Afghan security forces may never be known'. The Pentagon used the 'notwithstanding' exception to the Leahy Law to keep supporting implicated units, including approving continued funding in December 2015 for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.
cases.cover_up: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).

cases.title: Afghanistan — students report sexual abuse in Taliban-run madrasahs
cases.who: Taliban-run madrasah system (6,836 male madrasahs per a Feb 2024 UN report)
cases.what: In March 2024 RFE/RL's Radio Azadi published accounts from male students aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs in western and southwestern Afghanistan who said teachers pressured them and classmates into sexual acts and used corporal punishment; some left school. The report cited a February 2024 UN report counting 6,836 Taliban-established madrasahs for boys and a decree seeking 100,000 new madrasah teachers.
cases.cover_up: A 16-year-old said he reported a teacher to the school's qari, who only told the teacher to stop; the teacher admitted it and continued. The schools are run by the de facto Taliban authorities.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 9,941 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (3% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Moldova — children recruited online; institution leavers at risk (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers using social media and fake job ads
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers increasingly use social media and video chat to recruit children through fake job ads and exploit them in commercial sex, use abuse material as a grooming method, and target children in or leaving state institutions. Courts convicted 33 traffickers (22 for sex trafficking) in 2024.
cases.cover_up: A former police officer was convicted of labour trafficking (20 years); corruption and complicity remained significant concerns.

flows.title: Moldova → Russia, Turkey, Israel, UAE (trafficking of women and children, incl. institution leavers)
flows.what: The US State Department (March 2007) reported women and children trafficked from Moldova for sexual exploitation, increasingly to Russia and the Middle East including Turkey, Israel and the UAE; UNICEF found children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children.

flows.what: Amnesty (2004): international presence generated 80% of income for traffickers.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, nuncio to the Dominican Republic (2013): Laicised 2014; Vatican trial on child-pornography charges announced June 2015; died 27 August 2015 before trial Msgr Carlo Alberto Capella, Holy See nunciature in Washington (2017): Convicted by a Vatican tribunal 2018: five years and a €5,000 fine — not tried in the US or Canada Archbishop Luigi Ventura, nuncio to France (2019): Tried in Paris in absentia; convicted 16 Dec 2020, eight-month suspended sentence Holy See and the Murphy Commission (Ireland) (2009): No Vatican files supplied Holy See and IICSA (England & Wales) (2020): — Vatican files and Poland's State Commission (2022): — Lateran concordat and Italian reporting (2012): —

cases.title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
cases.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cases.what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.
cases.cover_up: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic

cases.title: Vatican tribunal — diplomat Carlo Capella and the Martinelli trial
cases.who: Holy See diplomat Mgr Carlo Capella; St Pius X pre-seminary
cases.what: On 23 June 2018 the Vatican tribunal convicted Mgr Carlo Capella, recalled in 2017 from the Holy See's embassy in Washington, of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years. In October 2020 the first Vatican criminal trial for sexual abuse began: Fr Gabriele Martinelli was accused of abusing an altar boy at the St Pius X pre-seminary inside the Vatican, and former rector Enrico Radice was charged with aiding and abetting.

flows.title: Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince
flows.what: Prince was appointed to Rome in 1991; a 1993 church letter discussed keeping him hidden in the Vatican rather than facing justice in Canada.

flows.title: Orán → Vatican: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
flows.what: After resigning amid clergy complaints in 2017, Zanchetta was given a post at the Vatican's patrimony office in December 2017; he was convicted in Argentina in 2022 of abusing two adult seminarians.

flows.what: The nuncio was recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; he was laicised in 2014 and died in 2015 before a Vatican trial.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2025: prosecution: Indonesian police bust ring selling babies to Singapore; 13 arrests (July)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Indonesia — baby trafficking syndicate selling infants to Singapore
cases.who: Syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers
cases.what: In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, some 'reserved while still in the womb', for 11–16 million rupiah each, after preparing fraudulent family cards and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested and six babies about to be trafficked were rescued; police sought Interpol help to trace the adopters.

cases.title: Indonesia — child sexual exploitation in the Riau Islands and 'contract marriages' in Puncak (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Foreign offenders; brokers of 'contract marriages'
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says extraterritorial child sexual exploitation is prevalent in the Riau Islands bordering Singapore, and women and girls are coerced into commercial sex notably in Batam. It also reports that Middle Eastern tourists pay more than $700 for week-long 'contract marriages' in Puncak, Bogor, involving girls as young as nine, a practice the government tacitly accepted. In October 2017 Batam police arrested a Singaporean man accused of molesting three boys (IBTimes, charged).
cases.cover_up: The report says the government tacitly accepted 'contract marriages'; corruption and complicity significantly impeded efforts.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Casa Pia (Lisbon): first report 1975, first action 2002 (27 years). A teacher reported abuse to leaders and police from 1975; police accused a caretaker in 1981 without action; diplomat Jorge Ritto had been removed as consul in Stuttgart (1969-71) after a complaint but stayed in service
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.0 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2022: Independent Commission for the Study of Sexual Abuse of Children in the Portuguese Catholic Church (Strecht), Jan 2022 - report 13 Feb 2023. 512 validated testimonies; a minimum of 4,815 victims; archives "the tip of the iceberg"
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. cases.title: Casa Pia — abuse of children in state care by a TV presenter, diplomat and others
cases.who: Casa Pia (state children's institution); Carlos Cruz (TV presenter); Jorge Ritto (ex-ambassador); Hugo Marçal (lawyer); Ferreira Diniz (doctor); Manuel Abrantes (Casa Pia official); Carlos Silvino (driver)
cases.what: Abuse at Casa Pia, a state institution caring for about 4,500 children, is said to have begun in the mid-1970s and came to light in 2002. cases.cover_up: A teacher reportedly began reporting abuse to Casa Pia leaders and police in 1975, and police accused a caretaker in 1981, without legal action. Childlight's 2026 update rests on representative surveys from only 60 countries; South Asia, West and Central Africa and the Middle East and North Africa lack them. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied 2023 data. In 2025, 14% of the 23.4 million reports to the US CyberTipline could not be placed in any country, and North Korea had 12. Countries with large churches and many children's institutions, such as Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, have held no national inquiry into institutional abuse in the sources reached. Where a country is colored only by estimate on this map, this is why.
